canberra.title: Canberra mother’s fury after anaphylactic daughter dropped from specialist waitlist
canberra.snippet: A Canberra mother has expressed her fear that children could die from preventable allergic reactions after the public health system kicke...
canberra.content:
Canberra Health Services’ outpatient specialist referral waitlist had more than 65,000 people on the books. Photo: James Coleman.

A Canberra mother has expressed her fear that children could die from preventable allergic reactions after the public health system kicked her daughter off the outpatient specialist appointments waitlist.

ANU academic Dr Liz Allen was shocked when a Canberra Health Services letter arrived in the mail, addressed to her nine-year-old daughter.

They’d been referred to the public paediatric allergy clinic in January 2024 after her daughter suffered several anaphylactic reactions – some leading to stays in Canberra Hospital’s emergency department.

The letter stated that Dr Allen’s daughter’s referral no longer “[met] the criteria for a specialist appointment with CHS” and that her referral had been closed.

“I’m gobsmacked this is how we would treat people in need … [families such as ours] are already under stressful circumstances as we have kids with higher health needs. To be treated like this – I’ve got no words,” she said.

“Our GP has since retired, so we’re now going to have to get all referral materials – including discharge materials from the emergency department – again.”

Dr Liz Allen was shocked to receive a letter stating her anaphylactic daughter no longer met the criteria for an outpatient specialist appointment at Canberra’s paediatric allergy clinic. Photo: Instagram.

On 8 October, CHS posted a statement on its website that it was reviewing all outpatient services so people “with the greatest clinical need” could access specialist care sooner.

There are about 65,000 people waiting for an outpatient appointment.

The paediatric allergy clinic’s waiting time is longer than six years.

Dr Allen questioned how children having anaphylactic reactions didn’t meet the criteria for “greatest need”.

“Essentially, what this letter says … [is] your kid, who could die from an allergic response, doesn’t meet the criteria to see a specialist and receive life-saving treatment,” she said.

“If kids with anaphylactic reactions don’t meet the criteria for an allergy outpatient service, what does?”

CHS outlined on its website that the criteria had been updated as suggested by the independent Walsh Report into the ACT’s health system.

Dr Allen said this letter was the only communication she’d received, apart from a confirmation phone call, since her referral was submitted in 2024.

She questioned how a decision could be made to remove people from wait lists without contacting patients to find out if their circumstances had changed.

“There’s no excuse for this, other than a willful act to very opaquely review systems without contacting affected people, and then change criteria without any [public] consultation,” Dr Allen said.

“This cannot be the way that a health service that operates in the most affluent Territory in the country … is treating its citizens.

“The risk is there could be children who die from preventable, preventable reactions.”

Dr Allen posted her daughter’s letter on social media.

Dozens of people responded, recounting their own experiences.

One commenter stated they’d been told at their son’s last appointment that he couldn’t be seen again for another four years.

“We were told … there’s no funding for the [sic] paediatric anymore,” they stated.

Another person who received such a letter for their daughter had been on the waitlist since 2018. One parent’s child aged out of the system while waiting for an appointment.

And from a professional: “6 years !!?? I am actually shook as a paediatric nurse.”

Dr Liz Allen took to Instagram to express her shock and outrage that her daughter had been removed from a specialist waitlist. Photo: Instagram.

Dr Allen said she’d also been contacted privately, including by a practising private paediatric allergenist who offered their services to CHS, but was told CHS didn’t have the money to pay for their time.

“The [people] and goodwill is there,” she said.

“So it looks like [CHS] can’t afford to pay for vital services – is that where we’re at? That’s life-threatening.”

Several said they’d resorted to going to a specialist hub in Goulburn, or even further to Sydney, for treatment.

Private allergy services are available in Canberra, but they can cost hundreds of dollars.

“There will be some people who simply cannot pay to go private,” Dr Allen said.

Opposition Leader and Shadow Health Minister Mark Parton described the situation as “shameful”.

“It exposes the chaos in our health system and raises serious questions about the advice given to the [Health] Minister,” he said.

Mr Parton will move a motion in the Legislative Assembly on Tuesday (27 October) calling on the ACT Government to honour the original waiting lists.

“We understand that they’re going through a process of review, but we don’t believe that that process of review should mean weeding out everyone on the waiting list and starting from scratch,” he said.

“I think we’ve seen over a number of portfolio areas that this government is not a fan of bad report cards, and they will do anything to change those report cards, and one of the ways to get yourself out of a sticky situation of having 65,000 people on waiting lists is to just crash those waiting lists.

“We don’t believe that’s acceptable.”

Independent Kurrajong MLA Thomas Emerson will also move an order for the production of documents (co-sponsored with ACT Greens MLA Rebecca Vassarotti and Mr Parton) for the government to table a number of 2026 papers relating to the Paediatric Allergy Clinic waitlist, complaints about the changed criteria, risk assessments undertaken before the change was enacted, and data relating to how the waitlist has changed in the past five years.

The ACT Government did not respond to questions in time for publication.

canberra.title: Rapist ‘monster’ who held woman captive for two days ‘deserves no mercy’, court told
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence. The violent rapist who inflicted an unimaginable ordeal on his young victim pose...
canberra.content:
Sisituutuumata Fulivai, 47, has faced the ACT Supreme Court for his sentencing hearing. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence.

The violent rapist who inflicted an unimaginable ordeal on his young victim poses a significant risk to women, a court heard when she and her family faced him in court.

Sisituutuumata Fulivai held a young woman captive at his home in Lyneham for two days in June 2024 while raping and repeatedly assaulting her. She eventually managed to fight her way out of his home and fled, naked, onto the street, where she was found by police.

“It was an eternity of a terrifying nightmare,” the woman, aged in her mid-20s, said this week.

“You didn’t just violate my body. You took a machete to my mind and my very sense of safety in this world.

“No person should ever have the chance to meet the monster I did. He is a danger to women and to society.”

The now-47-year-old Tongan man, whom the woman called ‘Matt’, was found guilty of 20 charges at the end of his ACT Supreme Court jury trial.

Her family had travelled for hours to support her when he was originally scheduled to face his sentencing hearing in June.

However, when they arrived, they learned Fulivai had fired his previous solicitors, so the sentencing could not go ahead and was instead adjourned to Monday (26 October).

The woman, who was visibly emotional, told the court she had fought desperately to survive over those days and was now living with crippling post-traumatic stress disorder.

“But the devastation of your actions didn’t stop once I escaped. Your violence bled out, infecting everyone who loves me,” she told him.

But the woman also told him the scars he left were the marks of her survival.

“I have reclaimed my life, my mind and my voice that you tried to erase in an attempt to destroy my identity,” she said.

“I’m far more resilient than you could ever comprehend.”

Fulivai watched on while she spoke. He tried to interrupt the woman’s mother when she started speaking to the court; however, Justice Belinda Baker told him to be quiet.

The mother said Fulivai’s actions had a profound and catastrophic impact on her daughter and their family.

“My vibrant girl is replaced with a shell of her former self,” the mother said.

“He chose to be inhuman … He was planning to kill my child.

“He showed my daughter no mercy; he deserves the same.”

Prosecutor Nathan Deakes said Fulivai’s abuse called for a significant term of imprisonment.

“Your Honour would find it was a protracted, extreme and degrading ordeal,” he said.

“It is the prosecution’s submission that the risk that this offender poses to women is significant.

“Any sentence must recognise the importance of protecting women from sexual violence.”

Mr Deakes noted Fulivai had received multiple sanctions for violence against other inmates during the two years he had spent in custody so far.

His barrister, Christina Muthurajah, said her client would eventually be released from custody and his rehabilitation should still be considered upon sentencing.

She said her client had been a contributing member of the community until a few years ago.

His life took “a sharp turn” in 2023 after he lost his job and his home. Until January 2024, he only had a minor incident on his criminal record.

Justice Baker reserved her decision and will sentence Fulivai, who remains in custody, at a future date.

He was found guilty of 12 counts of assault, three counts of choking, three counts of making a threat to kill, as well as single counts of sexual intercourse without consent and unlawful confinement.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Government contractor suspended after allegedly using job to stalk woman
canberra.snippet: While a man accused of committing a terrifying stalking campaign against a woman he barely knew has been granted bail, he won’t be ...
canberra.content:
Suyash Sinha, 31, leaves court holding his shoes after the court granted him bail. Photo: Albert McKnight.

While a man accused of committing a terrifying stalking campaign against a woman he barely knew has been granted bail, he won’t be returning to his contracting job at the ACT Government after being suspended due to his charge.

Suyash Sinha, a 31-year-old from Franklin, was charged with stalking and was originally refused bail when he first faced the ACT Magistrates Court earlier this month.

The court heard he found a woman on a dating app in January 2026, but when he asked her to start a relationship, she refused.

Despite this, she allegedly continued to receive messages from him during the year. Then, in August 2026, she was shopping at a Coles in Canberra when he allegedly messaged her, described what she was wearing, and said he was at the supermarket too. He had a second job at the supermarket.

The court further heard that as Mr Sinha kept messaging her, the woman became frustrated and agreed to meet him in person to tell him to stop.

When they met at a pub, he allegedly said he worked in finance for the ACT Government and told her the name of one of her siblings, which she had never mentioned to him before.

“Anyone could be looked up in government systems,” he allegedly said.

The woman was afraid and left.

In addition to allegedly continuing to message her, he reportedly also sent her multiple friend requests from different accounts on social media apps during September.

The court heard these accounts allegedly had names like “willbeseeingyousoonnoworry”, “riskingitallforyousexy [her name]”, “Ihateyousomuchgoodbye”, and “sexy [her name] forpresident”.

Mr Sinha spent about two weeks in custody before applying for bail for the second time on Monday (26 October), which the prosecution again opposed.

His lawyer, Satomi Hamon of CODA Criminal Law, said her client had a Masters in Finance and Accounting from the Australian National University and had been tutoring at the university as well as contracting at the ACT Government.

However, the court heard he was suspended without pay from his government job after his employer learned of his charge through media reporting.

Ms Hamon said her client had made various admissions when he was interviewed by police. But she pointed out the stalking allegations ended about a month before he was arrested.

The lawyer said her client had no prior criminal history and argued nothing suggested he couldn’t comply with bail conditions.

The prosecutor, when opposing bail, alleged the messages Mr Sinha sent the woman “effectively describe a person who is unable to take no for an answer”.

She also said police were still investigating his alleged use of government work systems.

Magistrate Ian Temby said the bail application was tricky. He said on one hand, the alleged messages exhibited a degree of “obsessiveness” and meant there was a risk of him endangering the woman’s safety.

But he also agreed with Ms Hamon that nothing suggested he couldn’t comply with bail conditions.

Magistrate Temby granted bail on several conditions, including that Mr Sinha not contact the woman or her family, not use social media, and not access any individual’s personal information in government systems unless required to do so for his job.

The matter was adjourned to 4 November. No plea was entered.

canberra.title: Will Murray: Wagga cult hero to worldwide fame after flood rescue
canberra.snippet: ABC reporter Will Murray has become a worldwide household name after putting down his camera and plunging into floodwaters near Brisbane ...
canberra.content:
26 October 2026

Join the conversation

1

Will Murray also got in the water when working in Wagga. Photo: Will Murray/Facebook.

ABC reporter Will Murray has become a worldwide household name after putting down his camera and plunging into floodwaters near Brisbane to rescue a man from drowning.

The dramatic rescue last Thursday (22 October) has made headlines around the world, with the BBC and New York Times among the international media outlets chasing the story.

But long before his newfound fame, Mr Murray had a cult following in Wagga, where he cut his teeth as a television journalist between 2017 and 2021.

Such was his popularity that a Facebook page called Fans of Will Murray was dedicated to his Riverina reporting, including his penchant for getting stuck into a story – sometimes literally.

Mr Murray was never shy about getting his feet wet, famously wading into the Murrumbidgee River in a shirt and tie while covering the cancellation of the annual Gumi Race.

Region caught up with the 33-year-old to talk about his split-second decision to jump into the water, his newfound international fame and his memories of Wagga and his cult following.

How does it feel to read about yourself in the BBC and New York Times?

Unbelievable and so weird. The BBC one was OK, I was measured. But by the time the New York Times called, it had been such an overwhelming day and I wasn’t proud of that interview.

But I guess it’s always better than being in the news for something negative.

Is Wagga where you really plied your trade as a journalist?

Wagga was my first proper TV gig. I worked in Canberra for a bit doing news updates and Seven Regional sent me to Wagga. I moved to Channel Nine a year later.

We only left Wagga because the local Channel Nine went belly up. My wife Liz, who also worked in media and I were made redundant and moved to Tasmania.

We loved Wagga and didn’t want to leave. I’ve never been involved in better footy clubs or a better community.

It was a massive news market. We covered everything from Culcairn to Young to Griffith. It’s an awesome place.

Will won a best on ground medal after a grand final win in the Riverina League in 2020. Photo: Will Murray Facebook.

You developed a cult following in Wagga and even had a Facebook page dedicated to you – how did that happen?

I was doing a lot of silly things on camera, so a friend of mine made a compilation and put it on a Facebook page dedicated to me.

Thankfully, it is now defunct.

Did you hesitate at all before jumping into the water to rescue the man?

It sounds cliched, but it felt like he was in a really bad spot and about to drown. At that point, everything goes out of your mind.

I thought, who cares about anything else? I could never watch someone drown.

Did you feel your life was in danger, too?

No, this wasn’t the Murrumbidgee. It wasn’t flowing heavily. I thought I could hold on to the fence if needed, but later realised it was barbed wire, so that wouldn’t have been a good idea.

How was the weekend after becoming a worldwide hero?

After the adrenaline crashed on Saturday, I felt really flat. The publicity was crazy. It was too much, but I’m better now.

How do you think your heroics will impact your career?

I think it will wear off really quickly. People have already forgotten.

Did you get time off afterwards?

I did get Friday afternoon off, but I’m back to work today (Monday).

Everyone in Wagga says you’re the ultimate nice guy and always so nice. Surely you’ve done something bad in your life. Tell us.

Just ask my wife, Liz.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: No time to waste as work kicks off on state-of-the-art recycling hub at Hume
canberra.snippet: The ACT is on track to save about $10 million a year, and maybe even make some money, as work officially kicks off on the Territory&#8217...
canberra.content:
Manteena CEO Mark Bauer, Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne and Veolia CEO Craig Barker turning the sod for construction of the new Hume Materials Recovery Facility (MRF). Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The ACT is on track to save about $10 million a year, and maybe even make some money, as work officially kicks off on the Territory’s new Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) at Hume.

It’s been almost four years since the original facility burned down on Boxing Day 2022 after someone put batteries in their red bin.

The fire meant the ACT had to truck around 50,000 tonnes of recyclables interstate for processing each year, at a cost of about $10 million annually. It also delayed the construction of Canberra’s Food Organics and Garden Organics (FOGO) facility (now expected to open in 2030).

Veolia CEO Craig Barker said delivering the $26 million facility would bring huge benefits to the Territory.

“This facility is where the ACT’s circular economy stops being an abstract policy goal and becomes everyday operational reality,” he said.

“When you look at a facility at this scale, the potential to process up to 115,000 tons here locally and, combined with our solar solution, we estimate around 26,000 tons of carbon will be avoided every year.”

Manteena and Veolia will work together to build the facility, with Veolia then running the MRF for the next 20 years.

Fire damaged or destroyed about 80 per cent of the Hume recycling facility on Boxing Day 2022. Photo: ACTFR.

The technology doesn’t exist yet to detect batteries earlier, but precautions will be taken to reduce the risk of another facility fire.

“When it comes to fire detection and suppression system … what we’re installing is significantly above the Australian standard,” Mr Barker said.

“[Technology for battery detection doesn’t exist] to the degree that we would like … but what we have is we have the ability in our contract, over 20 years, to innovate.

“So we will assess technology as and when it arrives to make sure that we can protect this facility.”

Both the ACT and Commonwealth governments have contributed $10.5 million each to the new MRF, and $5 million in insurance money will also be used.

The facility will feature high-speed optical-sorted, automated screens, and magnets to extract as many recyclables as possible.

A nation-leading feature will be the glass purification capability.

“[This] will allow us to crush and wash glass so that it can be used in re-manufacturing of glass products,” Mr Barker said.

“There’s not a lot of MRFs in Australia that would be able to wash and crush glass to colour grade.”

The old Hume Materials Recovery Facility has been demolished. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne said the glass washing capability would be a “game changer” for the Territory.

“Having a much higher quality glass product – [which] is highly sought after worldwide – we think this is something that we’ll be able to really be nation-leading on, and it will contribute overall to keeping costs down on this project,” she said.

“It’s going to be a world-class, state-of-the-art facility, one that has local jobs, brings recycling and materials recovery back to the ACT.”

The old facility could process about 60,000 tonnes of materials each year. The new hub will be able to recover almost double that amount.

Another aspect of the new facility will be the ability to once again see what Canberrans are and aren’t recycling, information that will support a dedicated education space at the MRF.

Veolia will invest $28 million in education over the course of the contract.

“[This] will allow us to make sure that the inbound stream is as clean as we possibly can, and then we can make sure that we end up with a really pure product at the back end that’s able to be recycled,” Mr Barker said.

Recycling Road will also be upgraded to improve access, safety and traffic flow within the Hume Resource Recovery Estate during construction and beyond.

Construction of the facility has been delayed for several reasons, including environmental approvals, the insurance payout and the development application process.

The new MRF is expected to open in early 2028.

“Ultimately, we’ve worked as quickly as we can while also ensuring that we’re future-proofing and delivering the best possible outcome for the Territory, with as many safeguards as possible, notwithstanding that we can’t mitigate all the risk,” Ms Cheyne said.

“This is a momentous occasion, and it’s one that’s been almost four years in the making.”

australia.title: Endangered turtles and ‘exceptional’ coral at risk from Woodside’s gas drilling in WA, watchdog says
australia.snippet: Exclusive : EPA flags oil spill risk from proposed gasfield and threat to pygmy blue whales Sign up for climate and environment editor Ad...
australia.content:
Woodside Energy’s plan to drill for gas off Western Australia’s north-west coast could significantly damage “exceptional” coral reefs and it may be impossible to reduce the risk of an oil spill to an acceptable level, according to advice from the state’s independent environmental watchdog.

A draft letter from WA’s Environmental Protection Authority written in 2023, seen by the Guardian, sharply criticised Woodside’s proposal to develop the Browse gasfield, saying its plans to protect endangered turtles and blue whales near Scott Reef would be ineffective.

Woodside, Australia’s largest fossil fuel company, is hoping to win approval next year to develop the Browse basin, about 300km off the Kimberley coast. Scientists have warned it could damage the Scott Reef ecosystem, which is home to more than 1,500 species, many unique to the area.

EPA staff presented the draft letter to the authority’s board for approval in December 2023. In February 2024, two months after it was discussed, the EPA sent a letter to Woodside saying its preliminary view was to reject development of the vast gas reserve.

It was a significant setback to Woodside’s plan to drill more than 50 wells and pipe the gas 1,000km to its ageing North West Shelf gas export plant adjacent to the world heritage-listed Murujuga rock art.

The company won approval last year to run the North West Shelf until 2070. But it needs the gas from the Browse basin – Australia’s largest undeveloped source of gas – to feed it. If the processing plant was to operate until 2070 it could lead to about 88m tonnes of carbon dioxide being released into the atmosphere each year after the gas was burned.

The concerns presented in the letter to the EPA board show the pressure on authorities to recommend against the gasfield development being approved. The development is being assessed by both the state and commonwealth EPAs. Ultimate decision-making power lies with environment ministers.

The letter shows the EPA board was advised by its staff that there was a threat of serious or irreversible harm to turtles and whales and more generally due to oil spills. The threats were considered serious enough that the staff said the precautionary principle should be invoked. It meant the EPA should assume the worst possible outcomes could occur.

In response to this near rejection of its proposal, Woodside added explosive-driven shear rams to its drilling plans, a step that could allow it to seal a leaking well in seconds. The company said this would reduce the “longest credible duration” of a “highly unlikely” well blowout, and potential oil spill, to about 12 hours.

Not all companies have faith in shear ram technology. In 2024, fellow WA gas exporter Chevron rejected “pyrotechnic shearing” technology for its own wells, describing it as unproven and impossible to test in the field.

A Woodside spokesperson said if the shear rams failed it would deploy a capping stack to stop the oil flow within 16 days.

But the EPA was advised in 2023 that if a well leaked for 13 days it was possible there could be “irreversible consequences” to Scott Reef.

The draft letter said Sandy Islet, a part of Scott Reef considered critical to the survival of endangered green turtles, would be threatened if the seabed subsided after Woodside extracted gas from beneath it. It said a proposal to top up the sand on the islet, where about 1,000 turtles breed each year, was a “high-risk” measure and its success was “likely to be limited”.

Woodside said it would address this by changing its plans so that no wells would be drilled within 20km of Sandy Islet. It also said the flaring of gas, which produces bright light that can confuse turtle’s navigation, would be restricted.

  • Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

The EPA board was also told noise, traffic and vessel strikes would have a significant impact on pygmy blue whales migrating between Timor and southern Australia. Scott Reef is the only known whale feeding ground on the migration route, according to the draft letter.

Woodside’s spokesperson said the company understood whales did feed at Scott Reef, but that this was opportunistic and the area was not as important as the ocean off Perth and other areas further south. Woodside agreed that Scott Reef and Sandy Islet had exceptional environmental value and it was important to protect them for future generations.

Glenn Walker, Greenpeace head of nature, said Woodside’s plans to address the concerns raised by the EPA did not go far enough and relied on “fanciful and unproven technology” to prevent a catastrophic oil spill.

“It would be a major backflip for both the WA EPA and the national EPA to now recommend approving this project,” he said. “It is now critical that these regulators maintain their independence from corporate and political influence and reject this destructive project.”

Greenpeace last week nominated Scott Reef for national heritage listing based on its ecological and scientific values.

Just two of the current nine-strong WA EPA board were in place when the watchdog told Woodside it was set to reject Browse.

One of those – the current chair, Darren Walsh – said in a statement the assessment had been lengthy because it was a complex project in a sensitive area. He said a final state report and recommendations on the proposal would be provided to the WA environment minister, Matthew Swinbourn, when it was complete. There would then be a three-week public appeal period before a decision was made.

A spokesperson for the national EPA said the development was being assessed under the national Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, and the “decision clock” had been paused while the agency waited on “further technical advice”.

Issues that have to be considered under national law include the potential impact on pygmy blue whales, green turtles, the marine environment in commonwealth waters and Murujuga rock art near the gas processing facility.

australia.title: How tall are the AI datacentre power poles that sparked a community backlash in Melbourne?
australia.snippet: Compare the concrete masts with their timber predecessors and other structures seen on suburban streets In something of a David v Goliath...
australia.content:
In something of a David v Goliath battle, Australia’s largest datacentre operator has faced a major setback in its plans to double the size of its west Melbourne facility.

To expand the size of its M3 datacentre NextDC needs to deliver increased electricity to the site. The initial approach from the electricity provider Jemena was to upgrade power lines along some suburban streets from shorter timber poles carrying lower voltage lines to taller concrete poles capable of carrying higher voltage lines.

But the upgrade has been delayed due to safety concerns, the lack of access to sites arising from community and stakeholder opposition, and because the local council had not approved 22-metre poles.

NextDC’s share price dropped from more than $9 a share down to $5.69 a share last week. The company and Jemena are looking at other options for supplying the increased electricity needs, including alternate locations for poles through industrial zones or connecting via underground power connections.

The site has faced strong opposition from West Footscray residents. Guardian Australia reported in May that residents were concerned about the scale of the expansion, the construction noise and the potential for diesel generators being used in the event of power outages.

Notes

The size of power poles varies, mostly according to the material used and voltage requirements. I’ve used sizes reported for the streets involved in the upgrade as examples but both types can vary. The six-storey building height I’ve used is based on an example of apartments in the New South Wales pattern book, while other building heights are approximated from actual dwellings. The brachiosaurus height is averaged from various sources.

australia.title: The chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costs
australia.snippet: Australia’s public debt may be well below that of France but there are lessons to be taken from its economic woes Get our daily political...
australia.content:
The explosion of discontent that led to major protests and violence in France and across Europe is a “warning signal” that Australia could follow the same path without an “honest conversation” about the budget, economists say.

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday to protest underfunded schools, as complaints of insufficient teacher numbers and dilapidated infrastructure mingled with broader discontent about cost-of-living pressures.

Here, and across the developed world, people are struggling to cope with the affordability crisis, as households grapple with high and rising prices.

The scale of the challenges in individual countries may be of a different order of magnitude, but the grievances are common.

Luke Hartigan, a senior economics lecturer at the University of Sydney, said it was clear there was no single factor behind the discontent in France, but soaring energy costs were having a major impact.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Fuel prices are up 36% this year in France, or three times the increase in Australia. The US-Israel war on Iran has sent European gas prices soaring as the northern hemisphere approaches winter.

More fundamental, however, is that France’s finances are buckling under its generous welfare state.

France’s high public debt, stagnant economy, and universal social security benefits have created a “binary” situation, Hartigan said, where citizens’ demands for better services and cost-of-living help are clashing with the country’s increasingly dire fiscal position.

France has not balanced its budget since 1974. Meanwhile, total public debt as a share of the economy has swelled to nearly 120%, according to the International Monetary Fund.

Australia’s total government debt pile looks benign in comparison at 53%. But a decade ago our debt was 40% of GDP, and a decade before that it was just under 10%.

Hartigan said France’s lacklustre economy had compounded its fiscal problems, underlining how Australia needed to work hard to boost productivity.

“If you think about trajectories, they [France’s challenges] give us an idea of where we could potentially be if we continue down this path,” Hartigan said.

“It’s a warning signal.”

Bob Breunig, the director of the ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, said there was a growing gap between what voters believed the government should be able to do, and what politicians were able to deliver.

“One thing that is happening everywhere is this narrative that the government should be able to solve all your problems, and that narrative has probably been pushed further in Europe than it has here. It’s failing in both places, but it’s pointier there than here,” Breunig said.

The evidence of this growing demand for government intervention is that French public spending now accounts for 58% of the economy, the IMF data shows.

In contrast, Australia’s total public spending is equivalent to 40% of our national output – the highest in data stretching back to 1990, outside the pandemic, and at similar levels to the United States and the United Kingdom.

“All these protesters are asking the government to help them out, but the government has maxxed out the credit card,” Breunig said, who said France’s debt was “reaching levels that are unmanageable”.

“The federal government here can still borrow and has a lot of flexibility, and the French just have no money.”

President Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power has been marked with failed attempts to rein in spending.

“There’s a real sense that people don’t know what to do,” Breunig said.

The bond market reflects growing alarm with France’s fiscal trajectory.

France typically has to pay a higher interest rate on its 10-year debt than fiscally prudent Germany, and the gap between the two rates is a measure of financial markets’ confidence in France’s fiscal position.

That gap is now at its widest since the European debt crisis in 2011.

Amid structural pressures on the budget from an ageing population, the NDIS, higher interest rates, and the push for greater spending on national defence, Breunig agreed there were lessons for Australia in not allowing the country to drift too far and for too long.

“We need an honest public conversation about what the government can be expected to do and what it can’t, and then a conversation about how much that would cost and whether we are willing to pay for that.”

While the opposition has attacked what it sees as the deadening effect of high government spending on economic dynamism, Breunig said he was broadly “agnostic” whether repairing the budget involved lower spending or higher taxes.

“At the end of the day, making these decisions is exactly what democracy is for.”

australia.title: Jacinda Ardern joins University of Sydney as lecturer and mentor
australia.snippet: Former New Zealand prime minister will focus on leadership, social cohesion and public health in new role The former New Zealand prime mi...
australia.content:
The former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern will lecture and mentor at the University of Sydney after moving to Australia earlier this year.

Ardern begins this month and her work will focus on empathetic leadership, social cohesion and civic trust. The University of Sydney said Ardern would be based in its school of public health, exploring ways to address global health challenges and focusing on equity, inclusion and wellbeing.

The former prime minister will host guest lectures and masterclasses and will engage in mentoring, but the university said it was not a full-time teaching role.

“I’m delighted to be joining the University of Sydney,” Ardern said in a statement. “I’ve found myself especially focused on the question of leadership since leaving office – and how we can better support and encourage the kind of leadership needed to tackle our many global challenges.”

The University of Sydney vice-chancellor, Mark Scott, said he had long admired the courage and humanity Ardern brought to public life.

“Dame Jacinda led New Zealand through events of profound consequence and her leadership demonstrated that empathy and resolve do not compete with one another; each can strengthen the other,” he said.

“For our students, the opportunity to learn from Dame Jacinda is exceptional. They will meet not only a former prime minister, but a thoughtful teacher with a great deal to share about public leadership and service.”

In an ABC Conversations interview in July, Ardern said she believed people were seeking empathetic leadership despite many world leaders embodying a “dominant style” of leadership.

“You see people voting for parties [that] are often on the fringes of the mainstream. When you dive into the research, the majority of those who are doing that are often not voting for the ideology – they’re just voting against the status quo because they don’t think it serves them any more.

“So I think all the signs actually point to people wanting something different than what they’re getting now.”

Ardern retired from politics in January 2023, after more than five years as prime minister and the leader of the Labour party. She led the country through the Christchurch terrorist attack, the Whakaari volcanic eruption and the Covid pandemic.

In 2017, aged 37, Ardern became the world’s youngest-serving female leader, later becoming the second world leader to give birth while in office.

Ardern has since held fellowships at Harvard University focused on public leadership and technology governance, and published her memoir, A Different Kind of Power, in 2025.

Ardern, her husband Clarke Gayford and daughter Neve moved to Sydney earlier this year, purchasing a property in Sydney’s northern beaches for $5.3m.

australia.title: Australians should prepare for online services to go down unexpectedly as threats rise, cyber agency warns
australia.snippet: Australian Signals Directorate chief says advanced AI tools are needed to defend against ‘AI-enabled attackers’ Get our daily political e...
australia.content:
Australians should prepare for more basic and important online services to go offline unexpectedly, the nation’s signals intelligence agency has warned, urging that “system security must be prioritised over system availability”.

The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) also says businesses and critical infrastructure must use cutting-edge AI models to defend against digital threats, raising alarm that artificial intelligence is enabling more dangerous threats than ever.

In its annual cyber threat report, ASD warns hostile foreign governments, criminals and hackers are using AI to gather intelligence, disrupt critical infrastructure and steal money, and that Australians should fight fire with fire.

“We need AI tools to help automate our defences to stay ahead of AI-enabled attackers,” the ASD director general, Abigail Bradshaw, said on Monday.

“Australia must accelerate the modernisation of its technology and cybersecurity foundations to protect the systems we rely on every day.”

The annual threat report, released on Tuesday, revealed that ASD had responded to 1,500 cybersecurity incidents in the 2025-26 year, an increase of 20% from the previous year. It also notified external entities – including businesses, governments and critical infrastructure – of more than 4,400 potential malicious cyber incidents, up 80% in a year. AI is expected to accelerate those dangers in future.

ASD said government and private networks in Australia experienced “persistent” breach attempts from state-based actors last year, and claimed such actors “in the Indo-Pacific” could be launching attacks to prepare for potential future conflicts – including “future intelligence collection or disruption activities”.

The agency said the increasing availability of AI was creating positive opportunities, but also allowing cybercriminals and state-based actors to find vulnerabilities and launch attacks faster and more effectively. ASD warned “all network owners are facing elevated threat levels”, saying cybersecurity was now a “core business risk and leadership responsibility” for all organisations, no longer only a technical concern.

The report said integrating AI tools into cybersecurity functions could help find potential weaknesses or suspicious behaviour, and improve responses.

“To strengthen our cyber defences, we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment,” Bradshaw said.

She has spoken previously about ASD having access to Anthropic’s Mythos model, the powerful AI tool which the frontier lab said it couldn’t release publicly because it could identify unknown flaws in IT systems. While the use of AI by malicious actors is on the rise, Australian government agencies believe having access to such frontier models and collaborating with leading AI labs is critical to bolstering cybersecurity.

“To stay ahead, Australians must enhance their cyber defences while harnessing AI’s benefit,” the defence minister, Richard Marles, said on the report’s release.

Tony Burke, the minister for home affairs and cybersecurity, said the government was “positioning Australia to respond to the evolving threats and opportunities presented by emerging technologies”.

Bradshaw said “legacy technology”, such as outdated systems or devices that were no longer supported with new updates by their creators, were among the biggest risks and most attractive targets for hackers. ASD called for Australia to modernise technology and cybersecurity capabilities, and said all organisations must take stronger action to ward off new threats.

Last week, newly discovered vulnerabilities in PHP – a programming language that underpins most websites – triggered a rush by governments and businesses to fix the problem.

ASD urged organisations to update their systems, seek help from ASD and report suspicious incidents.

Bradshaw and Marles said organisations should prioritise the security of their systems over keeping them online, which could mean more services are forced to go offline while they are secured.

“In a threat environment transformed by AI, collective action is our strongest defence,” Bradshaw said.

world.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
world.snippet: Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river wh...
world.content:
The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.

“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”

Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.

“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”

Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.

The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.

The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.

Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.

“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.

Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.

“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.

When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.

Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”

US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”

Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.

Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”

Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.

“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.

US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.

Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.

Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.

His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.

Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.

The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.

Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.

“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.

Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.

Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.

Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.

Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”

Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.

“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”

Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.

Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.

Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.

Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.

David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”

The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”

Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.

Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.

Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.

Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”

In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.

Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.

El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.

Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.

Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.

For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.

“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.

Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

world.title: Sudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern states
world.snippet: Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces hav...
world.content:
Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.

All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023.

The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis.

Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning.

“My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he feared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled. “We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said.

Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams.

Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.

In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.

Africa’s third largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.

The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services.

Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said by phone from Al-Junaid town in Al-Jazira: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again.

“We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land.

Farmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year.

To the east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”. “Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss,” he said.

Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and its currency has lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.

world.title: UK poised to miss reduced aid spending target of 0.3% of national income
world.snippet: Calculations from the Center for Global Development say spending next year is likely to be £410m less than anticipated The UK is on cours...
world.content:
The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.

Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.

The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.

However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.

Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.

Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.

The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.

The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.

The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.

Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.

She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.

“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.

“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”

Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.

The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.

The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.

The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.

The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.

An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.

“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

world.title: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
world.snippet: Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda Health officials acro...
world.content:
Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.

The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.

“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

world.title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix
world.snippet: 41-year-old set on ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’ Rwanda to host despite criticism of human rights record Lewis Hamilton has said h...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s. The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.

Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993.

Hamilton has been championing a race in Africa for some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.

“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that’s been my dream to be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”

Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.

F1’s deal with Rwanda is for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.

“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda is buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”

Hamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.

“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.”

The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Development Board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth. The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress and the Basketball Africa League.

Hamilton felt that at least the race would present an opportunity for people to take a greater interest in Africa.

“Going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there,” he said. “Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more of what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation. Then I guess I’ll finish it off with, I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”

Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli goes into this weekend’s US Grand Prix in a position to clinch his first F1 title. The 20-year-old holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton is fifth or lower.
